draft.title: Types of pathogens
card: Bacteria
single-celled living things. Most are harmless, but some cause diseases such as strep throat and tetanus.
Viruses
tiny particles that can only copy themselves inside the cells of a host. They cause diseases such as influenza and measles.
Fungi
organisms such as moulds and yeasts. Some cause infections such as tinea (athlete's foot).
Parasites
organisms that live on or in a host and harm it while feeding, such as head lice and tapeworms. Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they do not work against viruses.
draft.remember: Four types of pathogen cause disease. Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses.

a.q: Which type of pathogen can only copy itself inside the cells of a host?
opts: Viruses
Bacteria
Fungi
Parasites
a.why: A virus is a tiny particle that must use a host cell to make copies of itself. Bacteria are living single-celled organisms, so the most tempting wrong option, bacteria, is wrong.
a.clue: Think of the pathogen that is not a living cell.

b.q: Jaylen has a cold caused by a virus. His friend says he should take antibiotics. Why would antibiotics not help?
opts: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses
Antibiotics work against viruses, not bacteria
Antibiotics only work against fungi and parasites
Antibiotics work, but only after a few weeks
b.why: Antibiotics are medicines that act on bacteria. A cold is caused by a virus, so they do not treat it. The option that swaps bacteria and viruses is tempting, but it reverses what the card says.
b.clue: Which type of pathogen do antibiotics target?

b.best: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses

problems.detail: The sentence 'Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they do not work against viruses.' sits inside the Parasites bullet. A student could read it as a fact about parasites. It should be its own line.

'Four types of pathogen cause disease' suggests there are exactly four. The card only lists four examples, and other pathogens exist, such as prions and protozoa (sometimes grouped separately from parasites). Something like 'Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites can all cause disease' would avoid the overclaim.
